html:
The Gambia River, navigable by sea-going ships far inland, became a trade route to Europe after Portuguese sailors reached it in the 1450s. Alvise Cadamosto sailed up it in 1455.

Mande traders on its banks had long sold gold, salt and cloth inland. Europeans added a trade in captives, beeswax and hides, and later in groundnuts. Forts such as James Island guarded it. When Britain and France fixed their borders in 1889, the British colony was drawn as a thin strip along both banks, which is why the modern Gambia is a narrow country inside Senegal. The river still carries ferries and links farms to Banjul.
